---
title: "Gasoline Prices: Cleaning and Exploratory Analysis"
output: html_document
---

Only the supplied local retail and FRED spot data are used. No futures.
The supplied files are read directly from `data/` and are not modified.
This report covers cleaning and EDA only; forecasting choices are reserved for
seminar discussion. A calendar week is the unit of observation throughout.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "output/eda_", dev = "png", dpi = 120)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 1. Read data

```{r}
local <- read.csv("data/binghamton_weekly.csv")
wti <- read.csv("data/WCOILWTICO.csv")
brent <- read.csv("data/WCOILBRENTEU.csv")
rbob <- read.csv("data/WRGASLA.csv")

# Keep Binghamton only; the file contains other regions too.
local <- local[, c("date", "binghamton_average_gal")]
names(local) <- c("date", "local_price")
names(rbob) <- c("date", "rbob")
```

Local and RBOB prices: USD/gallon. WTI and Brent: USD/barrel.
RBOB is the Los Angeles spot series WRGASLA.

The averaging conventions differ:

- **Local retail:** a regional average of posted prices observed on Mondays,
  rather than an average of all seven days.
- **FRED spot:** weekly averages of available daily spot closing prices,
  dated at the Friday week-end.

These are observation/period dates, **not confirmed publication dates**.
Source definitions: [NYSERDA retail methodology](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/Energy-Prices/Motor-Gasoline/Weekly-Average-Motor-Gasoline-Prices)
and [EIA weekly spot methodology](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_spt_s1_w.htm).

## 2. Convert dates and sort

```{r}
# Remove the time part from the local dates.
local$date <- as.Date(substr(local$date, 1, 10))
wti$date <- as.Date(wti$date)
brent$date <- as.Date(brent$date)
rbob$date <- as.Date(rbob$date)

local <- local[order(local$date), ]
wti <- wti[order(wti$date), ]
brent <- brent[order(brent$date), ]
rbob <- rbob[order(rbob$date), ]

str(local)
str(wti)
str(brent)
str(rbob)
```

## 3. Check missing values and duplicate dates

```{r}
colSums(is.na(local))
colSums(is.na(wti))
colSums(is.na(brent))
colSums(is.na(rbob))

sum(duplicated(local$date))
sum(duplicated(wti$date))
sum(duplicated(brent$date))
sum(duplicated(rbob$date))

# Stop for review if dates repeat or existing rows contain missing values.
stopifnot(!anyNA(local), !anyNA(wti), !anyNA(brent), !anyNA(rbob))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(local$date), !anyDuplicated(wti$date),
          !anyDuplicated(brent$date), !anyDuplicated(rbob$date))
```

An absent week is different from an empty cell. Check both.

```{r}
local_weeks <- seq(min(local$date), max(local$date), by = "week")
wti_weeks <- seq(min(wti$date), max(wti$date), by = "week")
brent_weeks <- seq(min(brent$date), max(brent$date), by = "week")
rbob_weeks <- seq(min(rbob$date), max(rbob$date), by = "week")

local_weeks[!local_weeks %in% local$date]
wti_weeks[!wti_weeks %in% wti$date]
brent_weeks[!brent_weeks %in% brent$date]
rbob_weeks[!rbob_weeks %in% rbob$date]
```

Local data are missing December 30, 2024. Spot series have no missing weeks
within their own ranges. Do not fill values or delete unusual prices yet.

## 4. Merge spot prices

The three spot series have Friday dates. Join on those dates.
`all = TRUE` keeps all dates, even if a series has no value.

```{r}
spot <- merge(wti, brent, by = "date", all = TRUE)
spot <- merge(spot, rbob, by = "date", all = TRUE)
names(spot)[1] <- "spot_date"
head(spot)
summary(spot)
```

## 5. Exploratory alignment with local prices

Local dates are Mondays; spot dates mark weeks ending Fridays. We first pair
each Monday with the preceding Friday for descriptive comparisons. This retains
the original observation dates in separate columns; it does not change prices.
This is **not yet prediction-ready** because release timing is unverified.

```{r}
# Keep every Monday, including the missing local week.
calendar <- data.frame(date = local_weeks)
combined <- merge(calendar, local, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
combined$spot_date <- combined$date - 3
combined <- merge(combined, spot, by = "spot_date", all.x = TRUE)
combined <- combined[order(combined$date), ]
combined <- combined[, c("date", "spot_date", "local_price", "wti", "brent", "rbob")]

head(combined)
colSums(is.na(combined))

# Inspect incomplete rows; do not delete them.
combined[!complete.cases(combined), ]
sum(complete.cases(combined))
```

## 6. Save

```{r}
dir.create("data/clean", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(local, "data/clean/binghamton_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(wti, "data/clean/wti_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(brent, "data/clean/brent_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(rbob, "data/clean/rbob_la_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(spot, "data/clean/spot_weekly_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(combined, "data/clean/local_spot_exploratory_alignment.csv",
          row.names = FALSE, na = "")
```

No price values have been changed or filled. Keep the full history for now;
choose the training period later.

## 7. Price levels over time

Separate panels keep the original units visible. Missing weeks remain gaps.

```{r time-trends, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "output/eda_", dev = "png", dpi = 120)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(combined$date, combined$local_price, type = "l", col = "steelblue",
     main = "Binghamton retail", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/gallon")
plot(combined$date, combined$wti, type = "l", col = "darkorange",
     main = "WTI spot", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/barrel")
plot(combined$date, combined$brent, type = "l", col = "darkgreen",
     main = "Brent spot", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/barrel")
plot(combined$date, combined$rbob, type = "l", col = "purple",
     main = "Los Angeles RBOB spot", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/gallon")
```

## 8. Week-to-week price changes

Subtract the previous week's price. If either week is missing, the change stays
missing. This avoids calculating a two-week change across the missing local week.

```{r weekly-changes, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
changes <- data.frame(
  date = combined$date,
  local_price = c(NA, diff(combined$local_price)),
  wti = c(NA, diff(combined$wti)),
  brent = c(NA, diff(combined$brent)),
  rbob = c(NA, diff(combined$rbob))
)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(changes$date, changes$local_price, type = "l", col = "steelblue",
     main = "Binghamton weekly change", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/gallon change")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
plot(changes$date, changes$wti, type = "l", col = "darkorange",
     main = "WTI weekly change", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/barrel change")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
plot(changes$date, changes$brent, type = "l", col = "darkgreen",
     main = "Brent weekly change", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/barrel change")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
plot(changes$date, changes$rbob, type = "l", col = "purple",
     main = "RBOB weekly change", xlab = "Year", ylab = "USD/gallon change")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
```

## 9. Correlation: price levels versus weekly changes

Use a common complete sample within each table. Level correlations may reflect
shared trends. Change correlations describe weekly movements more directly.
Neither establishes causality or guarantees forecast improvement.

```{r correlation}
price_columns <- c("local_price", "wti", "brent", "rbob")
level_cor <- cor(combined[, price_columns], use = "complete.obs")
change_cor <- cor(changes[, price_columns], use = "complete.obs")

knitr::kable(round(level_cor, 3), caption = "Correlation of price levels")
knitr::kable(round(change_cor, 3), caption = "Correlation of weekly changes")
```

## 10. Time lag: do spot movements lead local movements?

### Why examine time lags?

Upstream and retail prices may adjust at different times. This EDA asks whether
local weekly changes are more closely associated with the nearest spot-week
change or with an earlier spot-week change. It describes timing in historical
observations; it does not estimate a causal transmission delay, select regression
coefficients, or determine the forecast horizon.

### Exactly what do lag 0, lag 1, and lag 2 mean here?

**Lag k means k additional weekly shifts after the initial Monday/Friday pairing.**
For a local observation on Monday 2024-06-17:

| Plot label | Local observation | Spot week ending | Date-label gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lag 0 | Mon 2024-06-17 | Fri 2024-06-14 | 3 days |
| Lag 1 | Mon 2024-06-17 | Fri 2024-06-07 | 10 days |
| Lag 2 | Mon 2024-06-17 | Fri 2024-05-31 | 17 days |

We correlate **changes**, not single prices. For example, lag 1 pairs the local
change from June 10 to June 17 with the spot-week-average change from the week
ending May 31 to the week ending June 7.

The general date-label gap is **3 + 7k days**. Ten days does not mean ten daily
observations, a ten-day training window, or a ten-day forecast. Each lag uses
hundreds of historical weekly pairs across the available years. The Friday is
an entire weekly average's end date, not an instantaneous Friday-only price or
a release date. These chart definitions differ from local-price ACF lags, where
lag 1 simply means seven days between two Monday observations.

```{r lag-correlation, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
lag_results <- data.frame()

for (market in c("wti", "brent", "rbob")) {
  for (k in 0:8) {
    # Shift the spot-change column down by k weeks.
    earlier_spot <- changes[[market]]
    if (k > 0) {
      earlier_spot <- c(rep(NA, k), head(earlier_spot, -k))
    }
    usable <- complete.cases(changes$local_price, earlier_spot)
    r <- cor(changes$local_price[usable], earlier_spot[usable])
    lag_results <- rbind(lag_results,
      data.frame(market = market, lag_weeks = k, date_gap_days = 3 + 7*k, correlation = r,
                 pairs = sum(usable)))
  }
}

plot(0:8, lag_results$correlation[lag_results$market == "wti"],
     type = "b", pch = 16, col = "darkorange", ylim = c(-1, 1), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Additional weekly lag / date-label gap in days",
     ylab = "Correlation of weekly changes", main = "Earlier spot changes vs. local changes")
axis(1, at = 0:8, labels = paste0("Lag ", 0:8, "\n", 3 + 7*(0:8), " days"))
lines(0:8, lag_results$correlation[lag_results$market == "brent"],
      type = "b", pch = 17, col = "darkgreen")
lines(0:8, lag_results$correlation[lag_results$market == "rbob"],
      type = "b", pch = 15, col = "purple")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("WTI", "Brent", "RBOB (LA)"),
       col = c("darkorange", "darkgreen", "purple"), pch = c(16, 17, 15), bty = "n")
knitr::kable(lag_results, digits = 3)
```

In this sample, all three markets have their largest absolute correlation among
lags 0–8 at **lag 1**. The correlations are about 0.45 for WTI and Brent, and
0.33 for Los Angeles RBOB. Under our calendar pairing, lag 1 uses the spot week
ending **10 days before** the Monday local observation, not simply one day or
one calendar week before it. These are exploratory associations; market changes
may persist across weeks and the strongest association can change by period.
The graph provides candidate timing relationships for later discussion, not a
chosen model. It does not show that lag 1 contributes information after controlling
for local history and seasonality. Pair counts vary slightly across lags and are
reported in the table; small differences in correlations should not be overread.

## 11. Local-price autocorrelation

ACF shows how the local series relates to its own past. The change-series plot
helps distinguish persistence in movements from persistence in price levels.
The dashed bounds are a rough white-noise reference, not a formal test of
forecasting ability. Missing calendar weeks are kept in place.

```{r autocorrelation, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(combined$local_price, lag.max = 12, na.action = na.pass,
    main = "Local price ACF", xlab = "Lag (weeks)")
acf(changes$local_price, lag.max = 12, na.action = na.pass,
    main = "Local weekly-change ACF", xlab = "Lag (weeks)")
```

All plots are exploratory and use the full supplied history. A lag selected here
must be re-evaluated using chronological validation on training data only.
Publication delays still need verification before forecasting.

```{r save-eda}
write.csv(changes, "output/weekly_price_changes.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")
write.csv(level_cor, "output/level_correlations.csv")
write.csv(change_cor, "output/change_correlations.csv")
write.csv(lag_results, "output/lag_correlations.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```


## 12. Seasonal patterns

### Question and preparation

Does the same part of the year tend to have higher or lower local prices?
A one-time jump in 2022 is not itself seasonality: seasonal patterns should
recur across years.

Use 2017–2025, the complete **calendar-year spans** in the supplied data; the
missing December 2024 week remains absent. Exclude partial-year 2026 only from
this seasonal comparison, not from the earlier EDA.

Subtract each year's observed mean to reduce differences in price levels between
years. Then calculate monthly means and give each year equal weight. This is a
retrospective display transformation, not a change to the saved clean prices.
It does not remove within-year trends or shocks.

```{r seasonal-data}
seasonal <- local
seasonal$year <- as.integer(format(seasonal$date, "%Y"))
seasonal$month <- as.integer(format(seasonal$date, "%m"))
seasonal <- seasonal[seasonal$year <= 2025, ]
seasonal$relative_price <- seasonal$local_price -
  ave(seasonal$local_price, seasonal$year, FUN = mean)

monthly <- aggregate(relative_price ~ year + month, seasonal, mean)
monthly_average <- aggregate(relative_price ~ month, monthly, mean)
knitr::kable(monthly_average, digits = 3,
             caption = "Monthly deviation from annual mean (USD/gallon)")
```

```{r seasonal-patterns, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 5, 3, 1))
colors <- hcl.colors(9, "Dark 3")
plot(1:12, rep(0, 12), type = "n", ylim = range(monthly$relative_price),
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "Month", ylab = "USD/gallon relative to annual mean",
     main = "Binghamton: monthly patterns by year, 2017–2025")
axis(1, at = 1:12, labels = month.abb)
abline(h = 0, col = "gray65", lty = 2)
for (year in 2017:2025) {
  d <- monthly[monthly$year == year, ]
  lines(d$month, d$relative_price, col = colors[year - 2016])
}
lines(1:12, monthly_average$relative_price, lwd = 3, col = "black")
legend("topleft", c(as.character(2017:2025), "Average"),
       col = c(colors, "black"), lty = 1, ncol = 5, cex = 0.7, bty = "n")

boxplot(relative_price ~ month, data = monthly, names = month.abb,
        col = "lightblue", xlab = "Month",
        ylab = "USD/gallon relative to annual mean",
        main = "Distribution across years: nine monthly means per month")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray65", lty = 2)
lines(1:12, monthly_average$relative_price, type = "b", col = "firebrick", pch = 16)
legend("topleft", "Mean across years", col = "firebrick", lty = 1, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

### Interpretation

- January–February average about $0.16–$0.18 below their annual mean, whereas
  May–August average about $0.09–$0.12 above it. This suggests a winter-low,
  summer-high pattern in price **levels**.
- The year-by-year lines and boxplots show substantial variation. In particular,
  2022 has a large within-year rise and fall; the average is not a rule followed
  equally in every year. This is evidence of a possible pattern, not a formal
  estimate of a seasonal or causal effect.
- Annual seasonality is compatible with weekly observations: each weekly date
  occupies a position within an annual cycle of approximately 52 weeks.
- A higher summer price does not imply that prices rise every summer week.
  Examine weekly changes separately before interpreting seasonality in changes.

### Are weekly increases also seasonal?

Group the local weekly changes by the **later week's month**, using 2017–2025.
Changes adjacent to the missing week remain missing; no values are filled.
Year-specific monthly averages give each year equal weight and show variation
rather than treating all weeks as independent evidence.

```{r seasonal-changes, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
seasonal_changes <- changes[, c("date", "local_price")]
seasonal_changes$year <- as.integer(format(seasonal_changes$date, "%Y"))
seasonal_changes$month <- as.integer(format(seasonal_changes$date, "%m"))
seasonal_changes <- seasonal_changes[seasonal_changes$year <= 2025, ]
monthly_changes <- aggregate(local_price ~ year + month, seasonal_changes, mean)
mean_changes <- aggregate(local_price ~ month, monthly_changes, mean)

boxplot(local_price ~ month, data = monthly_changes, names = month.abb,
        col = "wheat", xlab = "Month", ylab = "Mean weekly change (USD/gallon)",
        main = "Local weekly changes by month: variation across years")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray")
lines(1:12, mean_changes$local_price, type = "b", pch = 16, col = "firebrick")
knitr::kable(mean_changes, digits = 3, caption = "Average weekly change by month")

write.csv(monthly, "output/seasonality_monthly_by_year.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(monthly_average, "output/seasonality_monthly_average.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(monthly_changes, "output/seasonality_changes_by_year.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Positive and negative year-specific monthly changes overlap in many months.
The pattern in price levels is therefore easier to see than a stable month-by-month
rule for price changes. Market shocks can dominate seasonal averages. These plots
motivate further investigation; they do not establish forecast improvement.
Annual means calculated using a full year are only for retrospective EDA and
must not be used as if known during that year.

## 13. Do upstream–local relationships change over time?

Earlier sections summarize the whole sample. They do not show whether the
relationships are stable over time. We now compare **weekly changes**, which
are less dominated by common price-level trends. These are descriptive Pearson
correlations, not causal effects or estimated forecasting performance.

### Annual correlations

Keep the same Monday/preceding-Friday alignment (lag 0) in every year. Also show
lag 1, the additional one-week shift, as a sensitivity check. Missing weeks stay
on the calendar before shifting. Correlation is reported only with at least
30 valid pairs. The final year, 2026, is incomplete and is not directly comparable
to a full calendar year.

```{r annual-relationships}
years <- as.integer(format(changes$date, "%Y"))
annual_cor <- data.frame()
for (market in c("wti", "brent", "rbob")) {
  for (lag in 0:1) {
    upstream <- changes[[market]]
    if (lag == 1) upstream <- c(NA, head(upstream, -1))
    for (year in sort(unique(years))) {
      ok <- years == year & complete.cases(changes$local_price, upstream)
      r <- NA_real_
      if (sum(ok) >= 30) r <- cor(changes$local_price[ok], upstream[ok])
      annual_cor <- rbind(annual_cor,
        data.frame(market = market, lag = lag, year = year,
                   pairs = sum(ok), correlation = r))
    }
  }
}
knitr::kable(annual_cor, digits = 3)
```

### Rolling two-year correlations

Each point uses the preceding **104 calendar weeks**, including the plotted
week. Adjacent windows overlap heavily; fluctuations are not independent tests
of structural change. We keep lag 0 fixed to make windows comparable and require
at least 90 complete pairs within a window. Two years gives more observations
than a single year while still revealing gradual changes.

```{r rolling-relationships, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
rolling_cor <- data.frame(date = changes$date, wti = NA_real_,
                          brent = NA_real_, rbob = NA_real_)
for (market in c("wti", "brent", "rbob")) {
  for (i in 104:nrow(changes)) {
    window <- changes[(i-103):i, ]
    ok <- complete.cases(window$local_price, window[[market]])
    if (sum(ok) >= 90) {
      rolling_cor[i, market] <- cor(window$local_price[ok], window[[market]][ok])
    }
  }
}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 2, 1))
for (market in c("wti", "brent", "rbob")) {
  plot(rolling_cor$date, rolling_cor[[market]], type = "l", ylim = c(-1, 1),
       col = "steelblue", xlab = "Window end date", ylab = "Correlation",
       main = paste(toupper(market), "vs local weekly changes: trailing 104 weeks"))
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray")
}
```

### Whole history versus recent five years: descriptive comparison

The recent-five-year period ends at the latest supplied local date. Both samples
use lag 0, and neither is a training/test split. Similar average correlations
can hide changes within the periods. A higher correlation is not evidence of
better out-of-sample forecasts.

```{r history-comparison}
end_date <- max(combined$date)
start_recent <- as.Date(paste0(as.integer(format(end_date, "%Y")) - 5,
                              format(end_date, "-%m-%d")))
period_cor <- data.frame()
for (market in c("wti", "brent", "rbob")) {
  for (period in c("All available", "Recent five years")) {
    selected <- rep(TRUE, nrow(changes))
    if (period == "Recent five years") selected <- changes$date > start_recent
    ok <- selected & complete.cases(changes$local_price, changes[[market]])
    period_cor <- rbind(period_cor,
      data.frame(market = market, period = period, pairs = sum(ok),
                 first_pair = min(changes$date[ok]), last_pair = max(changes$date[ok]),
                 correlation = cor(changes$local_price[ok], changes[[market]][ok])))
  }
}
knitr::kable(period_cor, digits = 3)
write.csv(annual_cor, "output/annual_change_correlations.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(rolling_cor, "output/rolling_104week_correlations.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")
write.csv(period_cor, "output/history_window_correlations.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### Findings from the supplied data

At lag 0, whole-history versus recent-five-year weekly-change correlations are
0.376 versus 0.415 for WTI, 0.373 versus 0.395 for Brent, and 0.203 versus 0.208
for Los Angeles RBOB. The differences in these aggregate summaries are modest.
Annual estimates and rolling plots show larger variation within those periods:
for example, WTI's annual correlation is 0.428 in 2022, 0.098 in 2024, and -0.041
in 2025. Each annual estimate has only about 50 pairs, and 2026 has only 36.
This is a reason to investigate stability, not proof that older data are useless
or that the recent-five-year window is optimal.

These comparisons can reveal varying associations, but cannot by themselves
prove that the underlying economic relationship changed or decide a training
window. Differences may reflect sample size, unusual periods, volatility,
seasonality, or other variables. A later comparison should evaluate full-history
and rolling-window models on the **same forecast dates** using information
available at each date. No forecasting model is fitted in this EDA section.


## 14. EDA takeaways

- Prices share broad movements, but level correlations can reflect common trends.
- Weekly-change correlations and calendar-preserving lags describe historical
  timing more directly. Lag labels do not specify a training window or horizon.
- WTI and Brent are strongly correlated with each other, so they may contain
  overlapping information.
- Seasonal displays suggest winter-low/summer-high local prices on average, with
  substantial year-to-year differences. This is exploratory evidence only.
- Missing values, source-date differences, and publication timing must remain
  visible. Forecast horizons and model choices are outside this report's scope.
